fact: In Census 2011, Kerala's 1,017 inhabited villages averaged 17,179 rural people each; India's average was 1,395.
measure: Rural population per inhabited village (rural population divided by inhabited villages)
compare: India 1,395; next State Tripura 3,143 (5.5 times lower); 12.3 times the India figure
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 counts do not change; the next census (results expected from 2027) will give new village counts and sizes.
lead: 17,179 against Tripura 3,143 among States (447% more); Chandigarh (UT, 5 villages) 5,798. Census 2001 (checked): Kerala 17,283 against Tripura 3,093
size_effect: A rate (rural people per village), not a count; Kerala has 2.8% of India's people but 0.17% of its inhabited villages.
caution: The source states only counts; do not give a reason. Say 'villages as the Census counts them'. Use rural population only, not the whole State population.

fact: Between the 2001 and 2011 censuses, Kerala's towns rose from 159 to 520 while its inhabited villages fell from 1,364 to 1,017.
measure: Number of towns and inhabited villages, Census 2001 against Census 2011
compare: Census 2001: 159 towns, 1,364 inhabited villages; Census 2011: 520 towns, 1,017 inhabited villages; India towns 5,161 to 7,933
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026; Census of India 2001, Table A-01 (catalog 20028, read 13 Oct 2026)
stays_true: Both are Census counts; the next census (results expected from 2027) adds a third point.
lead: n/a (change over time, no rank claimed: West Bengal added more towns, 375 to 909)
size_effect: A change in Kerala's own counts, not a size comparison.
caution: Do not give a cause: the tables do not say why (Census towns are reclassified at each census by population, density and work-force rules). Say 'counted as towns'. The 2001 figures are in table evergreen/census2001_a1_states.

fact: Tamil Nadu had 1,097 of India's 7,933 towns in Census 2011 (13.8%), with 6.0% of the country's people.
measure: Number of towns (Census 2011)
compare: 13.8% of India's towns against 6.0% of India's people; next State Uttar Pradesh 915
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 count. The next census (results expected from 2027) will recount towns and many more will be added or reclassified.
lead: 1,097 against Uttar Pradesh 915 (20% more). Census 2001 (checked): Tamil Nadu 832 against Uttar Pradesh 704
size_effect: Share of towns (13.8%) is 2.3 times the share of people (6.0%), so not a size effect; Uttar Pradesh has 16.5% of people but 11.5% of towns.
caution: 'Towns' means statutory towns plus census towns, as in the A-01 table. Do not say 'cities'. India's printed total is 7,933 in this table; some Census summaries print 7,935.

fact: Arunachal Pradesh's 5,258 inhabited villages averaged 203 rural people each in Census 2011, against 1,395 for India.
measure: Rural population per inhabited village
compare: India 1,395; next-lowest Himachal Pradesh 345 (Arunachal is 41% lower)
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 counts; next census results expected from 2027.
lead: 203 against Himachal Pradesh 345 (41% lower). Census 2001 (checked): Arunachal 225 against Himachal Pradesh 313
size_effect: A rate. Arunachal has 0.88% of India's villages and 0.11% of its people.
caution: Pairs well with people-01 (Kerala's villages are the largest). Rural and urban area are not printed for Arunachal in A-01, but the population figures used here are.

fact: Only 10.0 in 100 people in Himachal Pradesh lived in towns in Census 2011; the figure for India was 31.1.
measure: Urban population as a share of total population
compare: India 31.1%; the lowest of any State or UT in 2011, next Bihar 11.3%
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 share; the next census (results expected from 2027) will show a new urban share.
lead: No rank claimed. 2011: 10.03% against Bihar 11.29% (1.26 points). Census 2001: Himachal 9.80% against Bihar 10.46% (0.66 points), which fails the one-point rule, so do not say 'lowest'
size_effect: A share of the State's own people, not a count.
caution: Do not say 'least urban' or 'lowest': the lead over Bihar in Census 2001 was under one point. Phrase as 'most of its people lived outside towns'. The share depends on how the Census defines a town.

fact: Mizoram was 52.1% urban in Census 2011, more than Tamil Nadu (48.4%) or Maharashtra (45.2%); only Goa (62.2%) was higher among States.
measure: Urban population as a share of total population
compare: India 31.1%; Tamil Nadu 48.4%, Kerala 47.7%, Maharashtra 45.2%; only Goa (62.2%) is higher among States
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 share; next census results expected from 2027.
lead: Second among States after Goa; 52.11% against Tamil Nadu 48.40% (third), 3.7 points ahead. Census 2001 (checked): Mizoram 49.63%, Goa 49.76%, Tamil Nadu 44.04%, Maharashtra 42.43%, Kerala 25.96%
size_effect: A share, and Mizoram is small (10.97 lakh people), so it is the rate, not the size, that stands out.
caution: Kerala's urban share was 26.0% in Census 2001 and 47.7% in 2011 (more towns counted), so avoid a 'Kerala' comparison beyond 2011. Do not say Mizoram is the second most urban 'place': Delhi, Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, Daman and Diu and Puducherry (Union Territories) are higher. Say 'second among States'.

fact: In Census 2011 the average district in West Bengal held 48 lakh people (19 districts); India's 640 districts averaged 19 lakh.
measure: Population per district (State population divided by its number of districts in Census 2011)
compare: India 1,891,961; next State Maharashtra 3,210,695
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: True for the 2011 district map. Districts have been created since then in several States, so do not say 'today'.
lead: 4,804,006 against Maharashtra 3,210,695 (50% more; Census 2001 district counts not compared); undivided Andhra Pradesh (3,677,425) left out because the 2011 count includes Telangana
size_effect: A rate (people per district); West Bengal is the 4th most populous State, but Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra are larger and lower.
caution: Always say 'in Census 2011' and 'districts then'. The lgdirectory.gov.in count today could not be collected (CAPTCHA), so no 'today' version exists.

fact: Chhattisgarh covers 4% more area than Tamil Nadu, yet Tamil Nadu had 2.8 times its people in Census 2011.
measure: Area and population, Chhattisgarh against Tamil Nadu
compare: Tamil Nadu 72,147,030 people on 130,060 sq km; Chhattisgarh 25,545,198 on 135,192 sq km
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Area (Survey of India) and the 2011 count are fixed; population has grown since, so say 'in Census 2011'.
lead: n/a (pair, not a rank)
size_effect: The pair is chosen for near-equal area (3.9% apart); the gap is in people.
caution: Population is Census 2011, not today's. Area is the Census/Survey of India figure. Do not rank the two States on anything but this size contrast. Pair: also Himachal Pradesh and Punjab (10.5% apart in area; Punjab had 4.0 times the people).

fact: Arunachal Pradesh is 7% larger than Assam by area, yet Assam had 22.6 times its people in Census 2011.
measure: Area and population, Arunachal Pradesh against Assam
compare: Assam 31,205,576 people on 78,438 sq km; Arunachal Pradesh 1,383,727 on 83,743 sq km
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Table A-01 (Number of villages, towns, households, population and area), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 count and Survey of India area; population has grown since, so say 'in Census 2011'.
lead: n/a (pair, not a rank)
size_effect: The pair is chosen for near-equal area (6.8% apart); the gap is in people.
caution: Area follows the Survey of India figure printed in the Census table (India's official map). Say 'Census area'. Population is Census 2011 only.

fact: In Census 2011, 77.2% of Goa's people said they knew two or more languages; the figure for India was 26.0%.
measure: Persons returning at least one language besides their mother tongue, as a share of the population
compare: India 26.0%; next Andaman and Nicobar Islands 67.6%; next State Arunachal Pradesh 64.0%
column: Share knowing two or more languages (%) [derived]
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Tables C-17 (bilingualism and trilingualism) and C-16 (mother tongue), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 count; the next census (results expected from 2027) will carry a new language question and tables.
lead: 77.21% against Andaman and Nicobar Islands 67.64% (9.6 points, 14% more) and Arunachal Pradesh 64.03%. Census 2001 (checked, all 35 State/UT files): Goa 73.36% against Andaman and Nicobar Islands 65.54%
size_effect: A share of the State's own people; Goa is small but the lead is a rate.
caution: Language knowledge is what the respondent reported (a mother tongue plus up to two other languages) in Table C-17. State the count only; no ranking of languages or States' worth. Do not publish a 'lowest' version of this fact.

fact: Half of Goa's people (50.8%) knew three or more languages in Census 2011; for India the share was 7.1%.
measure: Persons returning two languages besides their mother tongue, as a share of the population
compare: India 7.1%; next Chandigarh 30.5%, Arunachal Pradesh 30.2%
column: Share knowing three or more languages (%) [derived]
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Tables C-17 (bilingualism and trilingualism) and C-16 (mother tongue), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 count; next census results expected from 2027.
lead: 50.82% against Chandigarh 30.51% (20.3 points, 67% more). Census 2001 (checked): Goa 47.84% against Chandigarh 37.55%
size_effect: A share of the State's own people.
caution: 'Three or more languages' = the mother tongue plus two more, as Table C-17 counts. Say 'said they knew'. Pairs with the previous fact; use one or the other in a video.

fact: No single mother tongue was named by more than 12.3% of Nagaland's people in Census 2011; in Kerala, 97.0% named Malayalam.
measure: Largest mother-tongue group (Konyak) as a share of the State's population
compare: Kerala 97.0% (Malayalam); India's largest group 43.6%; next-lowest Andaman and Nicobar Islands 28.5%, Arunachal Pradesh 28.6%
column: Largest mother-tongue group, share of population (%) [derived]
source: Census of India 2011, Office of the Registrar General & Census Commissioner, India, Tables C-17 (bilingualism and trilingualism) and C-16 (mother tongue), read 13 Oct 2026
stays_true: Census 2011 count; next census results expected from 2027.
lead: 12.34% against Andaman and Nicobar Islands 28.49% (lower by more than half)
size_effect: A share of the State's own people.
caution: Mother-tongue groups are the Census's own groupings (Table C-16); the 'Others' bundle (12.2%) is many small tongues, so the largest named group is Konyak at 244,135. Count only, no politics, no ranking of languages. The Census 2001 mother-tongue table was not compared, so make no 'lowest' claim. Do not use the India (Hindi group) figure in a ranking: the Census groups many mother tongues under it.

fact: By Census 2011, one Lok Sabha seat stood for 27.4 lakh people in Rajasthan and 6.1 lakh in Sikkim.
measure: Census 2011 population divided by Lok Sabha seats
compare: India 2,229,936 (543 seats); Bihar 2,602,486; Uttar Pradesh 2,497,654; Sikkim 610,577
column: Census 2011 population per Lok Sabha seat [derived]
source: Election Commission of India, An Atlas, General Elections 2024 (2nd ed., Feb 2025), Table T3.1 (seats); Census of India 2011, Table A-01 (population)
as_on: Seats: 2024 general election (2008 delimitation); population 1 March 2011
stays_true: Until the Lok Sabha seats are readjusted after the first census taken after 2026 (Constitution, Article 82 proviso); the Census 2011 figure itself does not change.
lead: Rajasthan 2,741,937 against Bihar 2,602,486 (5.4% more); with Census 2001 population on today's seats Rajasthan 2,260,288 against Haryana 2,114,456, Uttar Pradesh 2,077,474; Sikkim is lowest among States (610,577; next Arunachal Pradesh 691,864)
size_effect: A rate (people per seat), so State size does not decide it: Rajasthan has 25 seats (tied 9th) but the most people per seat.
caution: Politically sensitive: state it as arithmetic with 'Census 2011' and nothing about fairness or cause. Seat numbers are set on the 1971 census (Article 81(3) proviso), a rule the Constitution states; the source does not link it to this gap, so do not claim a cause. Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are left out (2011 boundaries differ).

fact: The Constitution fixes each State's Lok Sabha seats on the 1971 census until figures of the first census after 2026 are published.
measure: Lok Sabha seats whose allotment to States rests on the 1971 census (Article 81(3) proviso)
compare: Boundaries of constituencies inside each State follow the 2001 census (clause (3)(ii)); the Lok Sabha has 543 elected seats, Atlas 2024 (ECI) notes the last delimitation was under the Delimitation Act 2002 on Census 2001
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department, Article 81(3) proviso and Article 82 provisos (PDF pages 68-69)
stays_true: Until the relevant figures of the first census taken after 2026 are published (results of the census due from 2027) and Parliament readjusts the seats. Check for any later amendment before use.
lead: n/a
size_effect: A rule in the Constitution, not a count.
caution: Politically live topic. Quote the text only: no view on delimitation. The constituency boundaries inside a State use the 2001 census (clause (3)(ii)). The text was read in the 1 May 2024 edition; confirm no amendment since.

fact: One Rajya Sabha seat stands for 6.1 lakh people in Sikkim (Census 2011) and 68.5 lakh in Rajasthan.
measure: Census 2011 population divided by Rajya Sabha seats allotted in the Fourth Schedule
compare: India 5,196,802 (233 seats); Sikkim 610,577 (1 seat); Madhya Pradesh 6,602,437
column: Census 2011 population per Rajya Sabha seat [derived]
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, Fourth Schedule (Rajya Sabha seats); Census of India 2011, Table A-01 (population)
as_on: Seats: Constitution as on 1 May 2024; population 1 March 2011
stays_true: Until Parliament amends the Fourth Schedule (seats there change only with a reorganisation Act or amendment); Census 2011 figure fixed, next census results expected from 2027.
lead: Rajasthan 6,854,844 against Madhya Pradesh 6,602,437 (3.8% more); Sikkim lowest, next Mizoram 1,097,206
size_effect: A rate (people per seat).
caution: Sensitive like the Lok Sabha version: arithmetic only. Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Jammu and Kashmir are left out (2011 boundaries differ). Rajya Sabha members are elected by each State's legislators, so the 'one seat stands for' phrasing is a ratio, not a vote.

fact: Three States were born within 15 days in November 2000: Chhattisgarh (1st), Uttarakhand (9th) and Jharkhand (15th).
measure: Appointed days of the Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar Reorganisation Acts, 2000
compare: Each from a different parent State: Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar respectively
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule entries 25-27 and footnotes (Acts 28, 29 and 30 of 2000), Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: Dates in law do not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date, not a size.
caution: Uttarakhand was named Uttaranchal until 1 January 2007 (Act 52 of 2006). Dates are the 'w.e.f.' dates printed in the Schedule's footnotes.

fact: Maharashtra and Gujarat were both created on 1 May 1960, when the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960 took effect.
measure: Appointed day of the Bombay Reorganisation Act 1960 (Act 11 of 1960)
compare: Gujarat 1 May 1960
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule entries 4 and 8 and footnotes, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: A date in law; does not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date.
caution: Both States still exist today in these forms; Maharashtra Day and Gujarat Day are both 1 May. Do not give a cause for the split: the Schedule gives only the Act.

fact: Haryana and Chandigarh both date from 1 November 1966, the day the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 took effect.
measure: Appointed day of the Punjab Reorganisation Act 1966 (Act 31 of 1966)
compare: Chandigarh 1 November 1966; Punjab and Himachal Pradesh's boundaries changed the same day
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule entries 16 (Haryana) and II-7 (Chandigarh) and footnotes, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: A date in law; does not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date.
caution: Haryana's entry was amended on 15 September 1983 (Haryana and Uttar Pradesh Alteration of Boundaries Act 1979) but the State dates from 1966.

fact: Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became States on the same day, 20 February 1987, under two separate Acts.
measure: Appointed day of the State of Mizoram Act 1986 and the State of Arunachal Pradesh Act 1986
compare: Mizoram: Act 34 of 1986; Arunachal Pradesh: Act 69 of 1986; both had been Union Territories
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule entries 22 and 23 and footnotes 4 and 5, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: A date in law; does not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date.
caution: The Union Territory entry for Arunachal Pradesh was omitted w.e.f. 15 April 1987 per the Schedule's footnote; the State's own entry dates from 20 February 1987.

fact: Sikkim became a State of the Indian Union on 26 April 1975, through the Constitution's Thirty-sixth Amendment.
measure: Effective date of the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act 1975, s.2 and s.4
compare: Sikkim has 1 Lok Sabha seat and 1 Rajya Sabha seat; population 6.1 lakh (Census 2011)
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule entry 21 and footnote 3, Fourth Schedule footnote 5, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: A date in law; does not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date.
caution: Use the Schedule's wording ('the territories comprised in Sikkim' were added by the Amendment); do not add a history the source does not give.

fact: Six present-day States and UTs date from 1 November 1956: Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Lakshadweep.
measure: First Schedule entries brought in by the States Reorganisation Act 1956 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956)
unit: year (six States and UTs share the date 1 November 1956)
compare: The same date (1 November) recurs in 1966 (Haryana, Chandigarh) and 2000 (Chhattisgarh)
source: The Constitution of India as on 1 May 2024, First Schedule (substituted w.e.f. 1-11-1956) and entries 1, 5, 6, 9, 12 and II-3, Ministry of Law and Justice, Legislative Department
stays_true: A date in law; does not change.
lead: n/a (dates)
size_effect: A date.
caution: Weak as stated: the 1956 Act reorganised older units (Andhra, Mysore, Travancore-Cochin, Madhya Bharat and others); Madhya Pradesh was reconstituted in 2000 and Karnataka was named Mysore until 1 November 1973. Several other States and UTs also date from 1956 or earlier but their dates are not footnoted. Use only if framed as 'reorganised on'.
